title: Ehud and Eglon King of Moab

named.name: Moab
named.label: right
named.site: the plateau east of the Salt Sea
named.note: Eglon king of Moab, with the Ammonites and Amalekites, defeated Israel and ruled them eighteen years (3:12–14). The Moabite plateau lies across the Jordan from Jericho; the plains of Moab face the city directly.

named.name: City of Palms
named.label: left
named.note: Eglon took "the City of Palms," Jericho by its spring (3:13; Deuteronomy 34:3), a foothold west of the Jordan. Joshua had cursed the rebuilding of its walls, so this was probably a settlement or residence by the oasis rather than a walled city. Eglon's "cool upper room" was probably here.

named.name: Gilgal
named.label: right
named.note: Ehud turned back "at the idols near Gilgal" (3:19) and escaped past them (3:26). The Hebrew pesilim means carved images or carved stones; some think of the twelve stones Joshua set up at Gilgal (Joshua 4:20), here perhaps as a boundary marker.

named.name: Seirah
named.label: right
named.site: unknown, in the hill country of Ephraim
named.note: Ehud escaped to Seirah and blew the shofar in the hill country of Ephraim (3:26–27). The site is unknown; the dot only shows the region.

named.name: Fords of the Jordan
named.label: right
named.note: Israel "seized the fords of the Jordan leading to Moab" and let no one cross, cutting off the Moabites west of the river; about ten thousand fell (3:28–29). The main fords near Jericho lie by the traditional site of the baptism of Jesus.

moves.text: Eglon of Moab, with Ammonites and Amalekites, crosses the Jordan and takes the City of Palms
Ehud brings the tribute down from the hill country to Eglon
After killing Eglon, Ehud escapes past the idols to Seirah
Ehud blows the shofar; Israel comes down with him and seizes the fords of the Jordan

symbols.key: Ehud kills Eglon in his upper room with a short double-edged sword
About ten thousand Moabites are struck down at the fords; the land has rest eighty years

p: Ehud was a Benjamite, "a man restricted in his right hand" (3:15). Benjamin, "son of the right hand," was known for its left-handed men (20:16). He hid a short double-edged sword on his right thigh, where a guard checking a right-handed man would not look, and asked to see the king alone with "a secret message" and then "a word from God" (3:19–20).

The Jordan can be crossed easily in only a few places. By taking the fords opposite Jericho, Israel trapped the Moabite force on the west bank. Gideon (7:24) and the Gileadites under Jephthah (12:5–6) later used the same tactic.
